title: Minimum finding: N classical queries vs O(sqrt N) quantum queries (Durr-Hoyer, bounded error)
problem_statement: Given oracle access to a table T[0..N-1], N = 2^n, of distinct values from an ordered set, output the index y such that T[y] is minimal.

input.parameter: n = number of index bits; N = 2^n table entries. The quantum algorithm is stated for n >= 1 (at n = 0 its implementation does not terminate; PROOFS.md §5).
input.size_measure: Query model: cost is the number of probes of T. The harness materialises the table (a random permutation of 0..N-1) only so that the oracle can be simulated.

algorithms.name: classical scan
algorithms.idea: Read every entry and keep the index of the smallest value seen.
algorithms.pseudocode: best = 0; for x in 1..N-1: if T[x] < T[best]: best = x; return best
algorithms.time_complexity: exactly N queries = Theta(2^n); N - 1 comparisons
algorithms.correctness: It reads every entry and keeps the index of the smallest value read (PROOFS.md §3). Optimal for exact algorithms when the values are arbitrary integers, since any unread entry could hold the minimum (PROOFS.md §3; on tables known to be permutations of 0..N-1, N - 1 probes suffice), and Omega(N) queries are needed even with bounded error (see lower_bounds).

algorithms.name: Durr-Hoyer quantum minimum finding
algorithms.idea: Keep a threshold index y (initially random). Repeatedly use the BBHT exponential search (Grover search for an unknown number of marked items) to find some j with T[j] < T[y], and make it the new threshold; stop at the time-out 22.5 sqrt(N) + 1.4 lg^2 N. Each new threshold is uniform among the smaller items, so its rank drops quickly.
algorithms.pseudocode: see implementation (the paper's steps 1-3, with its time-out and time-unit convention)
algorithms.time_complexity: O(sqrt N) queries in expectation (at most (4 + 1/n) B + 4, with B = 22.5 sqrt(N) + 1.4 lg^2 N the time-out) and success probability above 1/2 (PROOFS.md §5, Theorem 1); O(c sqrt N) expected queries for success >= 1 - 2^-c (c independent runs). As implemented: time-out B time steps; queries = 2 per Grover iteration + 1 per observed candidate + 1 (PROOFS.md §2); the measured mean is about 2 x the time-out
algorithms.space_complexity: n qubits plus the value register
algorithms.correctness: Proved in PROOFS.md §4-§5 for n >= 1: the element of rank r is ever chosen as threshold with probability exactly 1/r (Lemma 1); each exponential search with t marked items takes fewer than 9 m0(t) expected iterations, m0(t) = N/(2 sqrt(t(N - t))) (Theorem E); hence the expected time until y holds the minimum is below 0.95 m_DH, m_DH = 45/4 sqrt(N) + 7/10 lg^2 N (Lemma 2), and by Markov's inequality the time-out 2 m_DH gives success probability above 1/2 (Theorem 1). Credit: Durr & Hoyer 1996 (Lemma 1, Lemma 2, Theorem 1) and BBHT 1998 (Theorem 3), whose constant 9/2 is not used.

lower_bounds.bound: Omega(N) = Omega(2^n) queries for bounded error
lower_bounds.source: Proved in this entry (PROOFS.md §3), by reduction from unstructured search with one marked item: T[x] = 0 if x is marked, else x + 1 (distinct values, one probe of T = one query of the search oracle), so the classical search bounds proved in grover-search-classical-vs-quantum (PROOFS.md §5 there) apply: at least pN - 1 probes for success probability p. Credit: Durr & Hoyer 1996 state the linear classical lower bound (Section 1).

lower_bounds.bound: Omega(sqrt N) = Omega(2^(n/2)) queries for bounded error (Durr-Hoyer is optimal up to a constant factor)
lower_bounds.source: Proved in this entry (PROOFS.md §3): the hybrid argument of grover-search-classical-vs-quantum (PROOFS.md §6 there), applied to the tables T_x (T_x[x] = 0, T_x[y] = y + 1 otherwise), gives at least (pN - 1)/(4 sqrt N) queries for success probability p, and Omega(sqrt N) also for algorithms with an expected number of queries and success above 1/2, such as Durr-Hoyer. Credit: Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard & Vazirani 1997, cited for this purpose by Durr & Hoyer 1996 (Section 1)

relationship: QUADRATIC separation in the query model: Theta(N) classical queries (even randomized with bounded error) vs Theta(sqrt N) quantum queries with bounded error, all four bounds proved in PROOFS.md (classical: §1, §3; quantum: §3, §5; credit: Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard & Vazirani 1997 for the lower bounds and Durr & Hoyer 1996, Theorem 1, for the algorithm). Minimum finding contains unstructured search, so it inherits both the quadratic speedup and its limit. With the published constants (time-out 22.5 sqrt N + 1.4 lg^2 N, two queries per Grover iteration), the simulated mean quantum query count exceeds the classical N at every measured N up to 2048 (N = 4, 16, 64, 256, 1024, 2048) and is below it at the measured N = 4096 and 8192 (experiments/2026-10-07_minimum_finding.py, parts B and C).

background.statement: For non-distinct values the same algorithm works and the success bound still holds (Lemma 1 becomes an inequality).
background.source: Durr & Hoyer 1996, Section 3 (final remarks; read in arXiv quant-ph/9607014v2)

sources.title: A Quantum Algorithm for Finding the Minimum

verification.method: V1: both algorithms return the index of the minimum (independently checked against the table) on random permutations for n = 1, ..., 6, 8, 10, 12 (Durr-Hoyer simulated exactly with lib/qsim.py and lib/qsearch.py up to n = 10). Durr-Hoyer is a bounded-error algorithm, so its V1 agreement is a probabilistic statement; experiments/2026-10-07_minimum_finding.py observed 0 failures in 14000 runs (n = 2..10; one-sided 95% upper bounds on the failure rate 0.075% to 0.30%). V2 measures QUERY COUNTS reported through lib.qsim.Oracle: the scan uses exactly N (alpha = 1.000 against 2^n); Durr-Hoyer is fitted against 2^(n/2) over n = 4..12 with 5 instances per n (its count is nearly determined by the time-out: sd/mean <= 6% at n >= 4, so the predicted standard error of alpha is < 0.01). The fitted alpha lies below 1 because the time-out contains the explicit lower-order term 1.4 lg^2 N and each run adds about 75-100 classical candidate checks; over n = 2..10 the same measurement gives alpha = 0.800, inside the tolerance but close to its edge (see research/2026-10-07_quantum_entries.md). The experiment also checks the simulation against theory: the time and the queries of the paper's 'infinite algorithm' until the threshold holds the minimum agree with their exact expectations (computed from Lemma 1 and the exact BBHT costs) within |z| <= 1.01 for n = 2..10, and the exact expected time is only 11% to 27% of the Lemma 2 bound m0. Proofs: PROOFS.md proves every claim of this entry (the exact counts, the classical and quantum lower bounds, the analysis of the exponential search, and Durr-Hoyer's Lemma 1, Lemma 2 and Theorem 1 with the implementation's constants) and names the deterministic checks of each (tests/test_proofs_query.py, the experiment and count-check scripts).

caveats: A separation relative to an oracle, and only quadratic; it does not imply BQP != BPP. Durr-Hoyer has bounded error: Theorem 1 guarantees success probability above 1/2 (PROOFS.md §5; more with a longer time-out or repetition); the implementation is for n >= 1; the observed failure rate was 0 in 14000 runs, which bounds it but does not make it zero. Query accounting is stricter than the paper's time units: the marking 'T[j] < T[y]' depends on the value T[j], so each Grover iteration costs two queries (compute and uncompute, as noted by Boyer et al. 1998), and each observed candidate costs one classical query; the paper charges lg N per initialisation and 1 per iteration and does not count the comparisons. Because the time-out is a fixed formula, the quantum query count is largely set by design; the information in the simulation is that the minimum is found within that budget (V1) and that the time to reach it matches theory. With these constants the simulated mean quantum count was larger than the classical N at every measured N <= 2048 (N = 4, 16, 64, 256, 1024, 2048).
notes: Uses lib/qsearch.py (BBHT exponential search with an optional time-out), which is reusable for other amplitude-amplification entries. For non-distinct values see background; the harness uses distinct values only.
